draft.title: Projectile motion with vectors
card: A projectile moves under gravity alone. Take i as horizontal and j as vertical (up), and ignore air resistance. Then acceleration is a = −g j, with g = 9.8 m/s².
Horizontal motion has no acceleration, so the horizontal velocity stays constant. Vertical velocity changes at a steady rate of −g.
For a launch from the origin with speed u at angle θ above the horizontal: r(t) = (u cos θ)t i + ((u sin θ)t − 4.9t²) j.
Example: a ball leaves the origin with velocity 12i + 20j m/s. Then r(t) = 12t i + (20t − 4.9t²) j. It lands when the j part is 0 again: 20t − 4.9t² = 0, so t = 20/4.9 ≈ 4.08 s.
draft.remember: Horizontal: constant velocity. Vertical: constant acceleration of −g.

a.q: A projectile is launched from the origin with velocity 15i + 10j m/s. Which is its position vector at time t seconds, in metres?
a.why: Horizontal velocity is constant, so the i part is 15t. The j part is 10t − ½gt² = 10t − 4.9t². Using 9.8t² forgets the half that comes from integrating the acceleration twice.
a.clue: Gravity acts only on the j part, and the half matters.

b.q: A ball is thrown from the origin with velocity 8i + 14.7j m/s. How far horizontally has it travelled when it returns to j = 0?
b.why: The j part is 14.7t − 4.9t² = 4.9t(3 − t), so it returns to 0 at t = 3 s. Horizontal distance is 8 × 3 = 24 m. Using t = 1.5 s, the time to the top, gives 12 m, which is only halfway.
b.clue: Find t when the j part is zero again, then use the i part.

check.summary: No problems found. The card's formula and worked example are correct, and both questions have a single correct option that matches the explanations.

final.title: Projectile motion with vectors
card: A projectile moves under gravity alone. Take \(i\) as horizontal and \(j\) as vertical (up), and ignore air resistance. Then acceleration is \(a = -gj\), with \(g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^{2}\).
Horizontal motion has no acceleration, so the horizontal velocity stays constant. Vertical velocity changes at a steady rate of \(-g\).
For a launch from the origin with speed \(u\) at angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal: \(r(t) = (u \cos \theta)t\,i + ((u \sin \theta)t - 4.9t^{2})j\).

Example: a ball leaves the origin with velocity \(12i + 20j\) m/s. Then \(r(t) = 12ti + (20t - 4.9t^{2})j\). It lands when the \(j\) part is 0 again: \(20t - 4.9t^{2} = 0\), so \(t = \frac{20}{4.9} \approx 4.08\) s.
final.remember: Horizontal: constant velocity. Vertical: constant acceleration of \(-g\).

a.q: A projectile is launched from the origin with velocity \(15i + 10j\) m/s. Which is its position vector at time \(t\) seconds, in metres?
a.why: Horizontal velocity is constant, so the \(i\) part is \(15t\). The \(j\) part is \(10t - \frac{1}{2}gt^{2} = 10t - 4.9t^{2}\). Using \(9.8t^{2}\) forgets the half that comes from integrating the acceleration twice.
a.clue: Gravity acts only on the \(j\) part, and the half matters.

b.q: A ball is thrown from the origin with velocity \(8i + 14.7j\) m/s. How far horizontally has it travelled when its \(j\) component is 0 again?
b.why: The \(j\) part is \(14.7t - 4.9t^{2} = 4.9t(3 - t)\), so it returns to 0 at \(t = 3\) s. Horizontal distance is \(8 \times 3 = 24\) m. Using \(t = 1.5\) s, the time to the top, gives 12 m, which is only halfway.
b.clue: Find \(t\) when the \(j\) part is zero again, then use the \(i\) part.
